theme_scores.justification: Figures on life expectancy at 65 (13½ years in 1948, 18½ in 1995, 21 by 2007) carry ONS references 5, 6, 12, 13, 19 and 26, the Pensions Commission is cited at 20, and the DWP calculation behind the 27.6 years/41% figure (21) is only a bare attribution with no method; the uncertainty in projections (counted from the 'Wider ageing costs and projection uncertainty' theme) is acknowledged only in general terms, not assessed, so level 3 is not reached.

The dependency ratio (301 to 375 per 1,000) and the rise in pensioners (12.4m to 16.9m) cite ONS references 7 and 8, and the 1% of GDP/£725 per household figure cites the independent review (9, 30), with clear reasoning from pay-as-you-go financing to rising costs, but the £725 calculation is not explained and no assessment of the projections is given.

theme_scores.theme: Past delay and the case for a structured framework
theme_scores.justification: The historical account of unchanged pension age until 2010 and three Acts is largely uncited narrative, and only the 27.6 years/41% DWP calculation (Reference 21) is referenced, giving no method for it, so the theme stays at level 1.

theme_scores.theme: Wider ageing costs and projection uncertainty
theme_scores.justification: OBR projections of 7.9% of GDP age-related spending (5.7% health, 0.9% care, 2.1% pension) are explained, but only one cited line (Reference 31) supports them, and the uncertainty statements ('life expectancy projections are uncertain, and more so over longer projection periods') are acknowledged without any assessment of how they affect the case, so it stays below level 3.

reasoning: The two core themes that carry the quantitative case are well sourced. In 'Rising life expectancy' (level 2), the figures on how long a 65-year-old can expect to live ("13½ years, or 23% of their adult life" in 1948, rising to 21 years by 2007) carry ONS references 5, 6, 12, 13 and 19, and the Pensions Commission is cited at 20. A reader can follow these and see the direction of the trend and what it shows. 'Demographic shift and pay-as-you-go burden' (level 2) cites ONS projections (7, 8) and the independent review (9, 30) for the old age dependency ratio (301 to 375 per 1,000) and the 1% of GDP spend rise, and links them to the pay-as-you-go system. 'Past delay and the case for a structured framework' (level 1) is largely uncited narrative about the three Acts and the 1940 to 2010 history, apart from the DWP calculation at Reference 21, which gives no method. 'Wider ageing costs and projection uncertainty' is not core. The mean of the core themes is (2+2+1)/3 = 1.67, which rounds to 2. The strongest counter-example is the thin sourcing of the delay theme, and the DWP calculation (21) and the £725 per household figure have no explained method. The document does acknowledge that "life expectancy projections are uncertain", but it does not assess how that uncertainty affects the pension age case, nor does it consider contradictory evidence. To reach level 3 it would need to assess the quality and limits of the ONS and OBR projections, set out how the DWP calculations were made, and show how alternative scenarios change the diagnosis.
